tooSmall.title: This window is too small
tooSmall.body: Placeholder — write this text yourself (viewport.tooSmall.body in locales/*.json).

connect.title: Connect your device
connect.requirements: Works in desktop Chrome, Edge and Opera, served over HTTPS or from localhost.

demo.body: Runs the whole app against a simulated board, with no keyboard attached. Works in browsers without WebHID too.

demo.tooltip: This is a simulated board. No keyboard is attached.

unknown.title: No definition for this device
unknown.body: No registered board definition matches this VID:PID, so the decoded protocol is not used. If you have confirmed this keyboard speaks it, add a definition under src/device/.

notDecoded.title: {what} — protocol not decoded
notDecoded.body: This panel turns itself on as soon as a codec implements the command. Find the command with Explorer → Console → Prober first, then add a codec under src/protocol/.

apply.mismatch: {count} slots read back differently from what was written — the values below are what the board actually holds.
apply.mismatch_one: 1 slot read back differently from what was written — the value below is what the board actually holds.
apply.mismatch_other: {count} slots read back differently from what was written — the values below are what the board actually holds.
apply.failed: Not applied — the board does not have this
apply.appliedAt: Applied at {time} and read back to confirm
apply.noChange: The board already held this value, so nothing was sent.
apply.noWrite: The active codec ({codec}) does not support writing.

forced.label: ⚠ Forced: default protocol (development)
forced.notes: This device has no definition, and is being spoken to with the default protocol (raven61-v1) anyway. The commands sent are another keyboard’s, and what they do on this hardware is unverified. A write may damage its settings.

unknown.label: Not decoded (raw mode)
unknown.notes: The protocol has not been decoded yet. Explorer, console, prober and the traffic log all still work.

raven61.label: Raven61 (performance block and keymap read/write)
raven61.notes: Packet framing, analog key events, the per-key performance block read (0xa0) and write (0xa1), the global settings read (0x05) and the keymap read (0x08) and write (0x09) are decoded and hardware-verified. Every write is read-modify-write and is read back afterwards to compare the bytes. Advanced keys and macros are decoded from the firmware and both read and write are wired up, but not confirmed on hardware yet.

demo.label: Demo TKL (simulated)
demo.notes: Not hardware: a board simulated inside this app, 87 keys, tenkeyless. It answers the protocol decoded from a Raven61, so everything from codec selection to the read-back that verifies a write runs the same path it does against a keyboard. The values on screen are invented rather than captured, and are not evidence about any real board.

protocol.modeNoAck: The board did not acknowledge {command}; carrying on without waiting — {reason}
protocol.slotMapPartial: Only {found}/{total} keys were resolved from the keymap; falling back to the guessed slot mapping.
protocol.slotMapFailed: Keymap read failed; falling back to the guessed slot mapping: {reason}
protocol.emptySlots: {count} key slots are empty in the performance block: {keys}
protocol.blobSize: The blob is {size} bytes; it must be {expected}.
protocol.keymapNeedsSlotMap: The keymap was not read because the slot mapping did not come from the board. Reading it against the guessed mapping would show one key's binding on another, and editing from that would rebind the wrong key. Try reading again.
protocol.keymapLayerRange: Layer {layer} does not exist on this board. Only {layers} layers have storage behind them.
protocol.keymapUnsafe: The action bound to {key} is not safe on this board, so nothing was sent. The layer latches (0x04 and 0x05) make the firmware read another block as a keymap.
protocol.chunkNak: The board did not acknowledge chunk {index}/{total} (offset {offset}).
protocol.writeUnmapped: {count} keys have no slot and were not written: {keys}
protocol.writeMismatch: {count} slots read back differently from what was written: {detail}
protocol.writeNeedsKeymap: The write was aborted because the slot mapping did not come from the board. When the keymap read fails the guessed mapping is used, and that mapping does not match the real board — settings would land on the wrong keys. Try reading again.
protocol.globalNak: The board did not acknowledge the global settings write.
protocol.writeUnmapped_one: 1 key has no slot and was not written: {keys}
protocol.writeUnmapped_other: {count} keys have no slot and were not written: {keys}
protocol.writeMismatch_one: 1 slot read back differently from what was written: {detail}
protocol.writeMismatch_other: {count} slots read back differently from what was written: {detail}
protocol.firmwareEmpty: The board answered 0x03 with nothing. This firmware appears not to report its build.
protocol.resetNak: The board did not acknowledge the factory reset. It appears not to have started.
protocol.noAnalogMode: This board’s spec ({board}) names no analog test-mode command, so live travel cannot be started.
protocol.advancedRecordRange: Record {record} does not exist; this board has {max}.

reset.title: Factory reset
reset.hint: Puts the board back to how it left the factory. Actuation, rapid trigger, dead zones, the keymap, lighting, the polling rate and the debounce level are all overwritten with the defaults baked into the firmware. There is no undo.
reset.startNote: One press turns this into a confirmation. The same button has to be pressed again to reset.

confirm.title: This resets the board, and it cannot be undone
confirm.body: Every setting on the board goes: per-key actuation, rapid trigger and dead zones, the keymap, lighting, and the polling rate and debounce level with them. Neither this app nor the stock driver keeps a backup.
confirm.kept: Key calibration survives. The firmware's reset routine was read, and it never writes the calibration table at flash 0x20300 — what the board learned about each switch stays.
confirm.go: Press again to reset the board

stage.note: The same {seconds} seconds the stock driver waits, then the global block is read back. Do not unplug the board while this runs.

done.ok: Reset done — what came back matches the firmware's own defaults.
done.different: The board came back with values that differ from this firmware's defaults table.
done.unread: The command was delivered, but the result could not be read.
done.unreadNote: The board may still be writing flash, or re-enumerating on USB. This does not mean it failed. Give it a moment and read again from Board settings.
done.reread: The per-key settings were cleared. Read from the board again on the Input point tab to pick up the new values.

firmware.title: Keyboard firmware
firmware.hint: The firmware has no version number. What 0x03 answers with is the build's own name and the date and time the compiler stamped into it, so that is exactly what is shown here. Two builds made on the same day are indistinguishable, but the value does change across a firmware update, which makes it good for telling what is on the board right now. The stock driver never sends this command — it was found in the firmware's own dispatch table, and the handler (0x667c) only writes to the reply buffer, so sending it changes nothing on the board.

board.title: Board settings
board.hint: The polling rate and the debounce level are the two board-wide settings this keyboard has. Both live in the <c>0x05</c> block — the rate in the low nibble of <c>payload[12]</c>, debounce in bits 5-6 of <c>payload[15]</c> — and everything else sharing that block (the lighting effect, the game-mode locks) is written back exactly as it was read.
board.applied: Read the global block back after applying, and it matches.
board.mismatch: Read back differently from what was written: {detail}

rate.label: Polling rate
rate.warn: Changing the polling rate can make the board re-enumerate on USB. If it does, the browser loses this connection and you will have to connect again.
rate.writeLost: the polling-rate change may have re-opened the device. Connect again and check the value.
rate.note: What the four values mean comes from the stock driver's own list; it has not been confirmed against hardware.

debounce.label: Debounce
debounce.hint: The names are the stock driver's own. Neither the driver nor the firmware says what they are in milliseconds, so this shows the name and the raw value rather than inventing a figure.

force.title: Force the default protocol (development)
force.body: No definition matches this device. For a first look you can send the default protocol as-is and watch what comes back — ⚠ these are another keyboard’s commands, so a write may damage its settings. Keep the traffic log open.
force.active: ⚠ Forcing the default protocol. The key grid is a stand-in, not this device’s layout. Disconnecting clears it.

device.title: Device interface

unsupported.title: This browser does not support WebHID.
unsupported.body: Open it in desktop Chrome, Edge or Opera. The page must be served over HTTPS or from localhost.

known.label: Registered boards
known.hint: Only the vendor ids some device spec claims. Usually the one you want.

all.label: All HID devices
all.hint: For when nothing shows up above. Lists every HID device Chrome can reach.

vendorPages.label: Vendor-defined pages
vendorPages.hint: Only the usage pages commonly used as a configuration channel.

device.wrongInterface: The interface currently open does not look like the configuration channel. Open the one marked recommended in the list below, or no key travel will reach the monitor.
device.knownHint: Interfaces you have already granted access to. One keyboard showing up as several is normal, and only one of them carries configuration and the monitor stream — the recommended one with the highest score.

switch.title: Switch
switch.unread: Not read from the board yet. The values below are this app's defaults, not what the hardware holds.
switch.deeper: {count} key(s) are set deeper than this switch can travel. Fix them in the Actuation panel.
switch.unknownValue: The board holds value {value}, which is not in the table. Picking from the list overwrites it.

actuation.title: Actuation point
actuation.counts: mm = {counts} counts (in steps of {step} mm) · out of {travel} mm total travel
actuation.travelNote: The maximum is the total travel of the switch fitted to the selected keys ({travel} mm).
actuation.unread: The board has not been read yet. Read it in "Current board settings" above, then adjust.
actuation.deeperThanTravel: {count} keys have an actuation point deeper than their switch travel.
actuation.deeperThanTravel_one: 1 key has an actuation point deeper than its switch travel.
actuation.deeperThanTravel_other: {count} keys have an actuation point deeper than their switch travel.

rt.title: Rapid trigger
rt.enable: Enable rapid trigger on the selected keys
rt.continuous: Continuous mode (works above the actuation point too)
rt.noise: The board's smallest step is {step} mm, and the factory default is 0.10 mm for both press and release. Going below that can let sensor noise through as real input, so check the resting jitter on the Monitor tab first.
rt.belowFactory: {count} keys have a sensitivity below the factory default of {mm} mm. Resting sensor noise can come through as real input.
rt.noRoom: {count} keys have no stroke left for rapid trigger to work in — the sensitivity is wider than what remains below the actuation point. Turn on continuous mode or reduce the sensitivity.
rt.belowFactory_one: 1 key has a sensitivity below the factory default of {mm} mm. Resting sensor noise can come through as real input.
rt.belowFactory_other: {count} keys have a sensitivity below the factory default of {mm} mm. Resting sensor noise can come through as real input.
rt.noRoom_one: 1 key has no stroke left for rapid trigger to work in — the sensitivity is wider than what remains below the actuation point. Turn on continuous mode or reduce the sensitivity.
rt.noRoom_other: {count} keys have no stroke left for rapid trigger to work in — the sensitivity is wider than what remains below the actuation point. Turn on continuous mode or reduce the sensitivity.

deadzone.title: Dead zone
deadzone.hint: The stretch at each end of the stroke that is ignored. Same as the stock driver's Top / Bottom dead zone.
deadzone.enable: Enable dead zone on the selected keys
deadzone.limit: The field is 5 bits, so {mm} mm ({counts} counts) is the maximum. Past that the value wraps.

advanced.title: Advanced keys (DKS · TGL · MT · RS · SOCD · OKS)
advanced.note: A record holds the parameters and a keymap entry says which key runs it, which of the six kinds it is, and for RS, SOCD and OKS which key it is paired with. So applying writes twice: the record first, then the keymap.
advanced.unverified: The three tables and all six kinds are decoded from the firmware, and every write here is read back and compared — but none of it has been confirmed on hardware. A verified write means the bytes are in the table; whether the key behaves is what you are testing.
advanced.pickKey: Pick a key on the grid.
advanced.unbound: The key is back to its factory binding, and record #{record} was cleared.
advanced.unboundShared: The key is back to its factory binding. Record #{record} was left alone — another key still uses it.
advanced.unbindUnavailable: The board's factory table has no binding for this key, so there is nothing to put back.
advanced.applied: Record #{record} written, and the key bound to it as {kind}.
advanced.mismatch: Record #{record} did not read back as written: {wanted} → {got}. The keymap was left alone.
advanced.keymapMismatch: The record was written, but the keymap entry did not read back as sent: {detail}. The key is not bound to it.
advanced.noFreeRecord: All {limit} records are in use. Free one by unbinding the key that uses it.
advanced.noneBound: No key on this layer is bound to an advanced key.
advanced.orphans: Records with bytes in them that no layer points at: {records}. Left alone — from here a leftover and a record the stock driver wrote look the same.

dks.help: Four depth points and four bindings. Each binding goes down at one point and comes up at another; setting both to the same point makes it a tap. Points 1 and 2 are tested pressing down, points 3 and 4 coming back up.

tgl.help: Press once and the key stays down; press again and it comes up. The board can hold 32 toggles down at a time.

mt.help: Tap for one binding, hold for another. The hold time goes in the keymap entry, in units of 10 ms.

rs.help: Two keys, and whichever is pressed deeper wins. Give the other key its own record too, with this key's slot as its partner.

socd.help: Two keys on the same axis, resolved so they never fight. Give the other key its own record too, with this key's slot as its partner.
socd.modeNote: The resolution mode is not in this table — the firmware reads it from the high nibble of this key's performance record, which the input-point tab owns. Set it there.

oks.help: The key sends one usage while it is held and fires another when it comes up.

pair.partnerSlotNote: The other key's slot, as the table below reports it.

calibration.tableUnsupported: This board’s codec cannot read the calibration table, so the pass runs from the event stream alone.
calibration.title: Bottom-out calibration
calibration.gridLegend: Calibration progress — the border is the board’s LED, the number is the key’s calibration scale, the fill is how deep it went.
calibration.blocked: Tab switching and disconnecting are locked while calibration runs — leaving the mode is what lets the board type again.

health.uncalibrated: Never calibrated (scale still at the 0.62 floor)
health.weak: Barely calibrated — press it all the way down

calibration.copyDump: Copy the numbers (per-key scale and firmware state)
calibration.ledMirror: Keys the board is lighting right now: {lit}.
calibration.tableFailed: Could not read the board’s stored calibration table (command 0xaa). The pass still works, but keys nobody has pressed yet will have nothing to show.
calibration.ledDisagreeNote: LED colours are the firmware’s own palette: red {red}, amber {amber}. Dark on an uncalibrated key means the firmware latched "calibrated" too early; lit on a calibrated key means its state byte never left the value it shipped with.

ledState.red: Red — the board has never committed a scale for this key (state 0x00)
ledState.green: Green — the board calls this key done. On the keyboard itself the override simply stops and the lighting effect shows through

calibration.gridNote: The border is the board’s own LED, so the screen and the keyboard on the desk always agree. What that colour counts is how many times the scale was committed, not how good it is: a fresh firmware shows every key red however well calibrated, and two shallow presses turn one green. The number on the cap is the honest one — a scale of 0.62 means the key has never been calibrated.
calibration.ledDisagreeTitle: Keys where the board’s LED and the scale disagree (debug mode only)

perf.title: Current board settings
perf.needDevice: Once a device is connected, all {keys} keys are read back from the board. Connect one from the Device tab first.
perf.bottomOutNote: This one is a global setting rather than a per-key one (0x05 block, payload[15] bit 1).
perf.sameByte: Same byte: Tachyon {tachyon} · actuation_check {actuationCheck} · magnet test {magnetTest} · debounce {debounce}
perf.uniform: Every key has the same settings

emptySlots.note: An all-zero record decodes as actuation {mm} mm · RT off · {switchName}. That is not a real setting — it is a failed read.

perf.footnote: Values are in mm and the board's smallest step is {step} mm. The table shows what was read from the board as-is; edits made in the panels below do nothing until you apply to board.

keymap.pickNone: Click a cap to pick a key
keymap.unread: Not read from the board yet. Read it first to see what is bound now.
keymap.layerNote: This board has storage for two layers. The firmware indexes four, but layers 2 and 3 land on the per-key RGB and macro areas. Only a key action such as Fn changes the layer — the host cannot. A write edits the 512 bytes the board just returned, sends them back, then reads them again and compares.
keymap.unmapped: {count} keys have no slot, so they could not be read or written: {keys}
keymap.applied: Applied {count} keys and read them back to check
keymap.noChange: The board already holds these bytes, so nothing was sent.
keymap.mismatch: {count} slots did not read back as written: {detail}
keymap.resetUnavailable: The factory keymap read does not reach this slot, so it cannot be reset.

picker.title: Binding
picker.empty: Pick a key on the grid

keymap.trnsNote: KC_TRNS is not a record this board has. Its firmware has no transparent key, so this button copies the base layer's binding into this key. It is a copy and not a link: a later edit to the base layer does not follow it.
keymap.writeNote: The keymap command is usually long enough to be split across several reports. Change one key in the stock driver, save, and diff the captures: the byte that moved is that key's index — the most reliable way to work out the matrix order.

overview.todo: This tab is a placeholder — the feature has not been built yet.

macro.note: This board's spec names no macro-store commands. If the same commands answer on another board, say so in its spec.
macro.title: Macros
macro.unverified: The format is decoded from the firmware and confirmed field by field against the stock driver's own encoder — the record layout, the stop and press bits, the mask-versus-usage split and the millisecond unit all agree at both ends. Writes are read back and compared like every other block here, so the bytes are in the store; whether the board plays them has not been confirmed on hardware.
macro.storeReady: All 32 slots name a body and every body stops. Binding a macro key is safe.
macro.storeUnsafe: ⚠ Slots with no body or no stop record: {slots}. The player has no bound on its cursor, so pressing a macro key in this state sends it walking through flash four bytes at a time, emitting a keystroke for every record it passes. Write the store first — binding stays refused until you do.
macro.capacity: {used} of {total} events — what is left after the offset table and the one stop record each slot carries.
macro.slotNumbering: Slots count from 0. The stock driver shows {stock} of them, and its "M 1" is #0 here.
macro.overStock: Past the stock driver's recording budget of {total} events. The firmware and this block hold more, but the stock driver may not handle a store this size if you go back to it.
macro.name: Name
macro.nameNote: Names stay in this browser. The store is an offset table and 4-byte records with no room for one — the stock driver keeps its own in its database for the same reason. What identifies a macro to the board is its slot number.
macro.noEvents: This slot is empty. Record one below, or add keys by hand. An empty slot is still written with a stop record, so pressing it does nothing.
macro.recordingNow: Recording — the keys you press now go into this list instead of to the page. The gap between two keystrokes is rounded and stored as the delay on the earlier event.
macro.recordNote: Browsers never report Fn: the keyboard's own firmware consumes it and no key event reaches the page. Auto-repeat is dropped too — the board has no concept of it, and a held key would fill the store.
macro.modifierNote: Modifiers ({mods}) go out as a mask record automatically. The player's key arm puts its value in the report's usage array, and a Shift that arrives there is not a Shift to the host.
macro.repeatNote: The keymap record's repeat byte is never read by the firmware — macroStart stores it at gp-0x781 and nothing in the image reads that byte back. So a repeat is more records in the body, which is what this does. The stock driver's play_times does not reach the store either — its encoder walks each record list exactly once, so the bytes on the board carry no repeat count anywhere.
macro.applied: Applied to {slots} of 32 slots — {bytes} bytes sent, and the read-back matched byte for byte.
macro.unchanged: The board already held these bodies, so nothing was sent.
macro.capacityFull: The store holds {total} event records and this needs {used}. Shorten it and apply again.
macro.mismatch: Slots did not read back as written — {detail}
macro.keymapMismatch: The keymap record did not read back as written — {detail}
macro.pickKey: Pick a key in the grid above.
macro.bindNeedsStore: The store is not safe yet. Write it first.
macro.bindNote: Binding is the second write — the body has to be in the store first. That is also why the remap tab's picker offers no macros: binding from a tab that cannot check the store would be the one way around this order. A macro that is already bound does show up there by name.
macro.unbindUnavailable: The board returned no factory record for this key, so there is nothing to put back.
macro.unbound: {key} no longer starts a macro. The body is still in the store.
macro.noneBound: No key on this layer starts a macro.
macro.repeatByteNote: The repeat byte is read only. The firmware never uses it, so this app writes the stock driver's 1 — and reports whatever a slot already holds, so a store the stock driver wrote does not look misread.

light.title: Per-key colour
light.colorfulHint: The effect walks the hue wheel instead of using one colour. With this on, the palette below is ignored.
light.colorOverridden: not used while colours are cycling

dir.note: The stock page renames this pair per effect (within/outside, clockwise/anticlockwise, and two more). Which bit selects which pair is not established, so these are neutral — the byte is the same either way.

fxPanel.title: Lighting effect
fxPanel.unread: The settings block has not been read from the board yet.
fxPanel.unknownMode: The board reports mode {mode}, which this table has no row for. Left as it is — overwriting it with a value we do know would throw away whatever it was set to.
fxPanel.perKey: Custom Light is the effect that paints the per-key colours stored on the board. Paint them in the section next to this one.
fxPanel.raw: <c>payload[16..24]</c> = {bytes} · colorindex {index} (undecoded; the board's own byte is written back)

showsIn.title: When these colours show
showsIn.active: The effect is Custom Light right now, so what you paint here is what the LEDs show.
showsIn.body: Exactly one effect reads this block: Custom Light (mode 0). Every other effect generates its own colours and never looks at this layer — so with another effect running, painting here and applying changes nothing on the keyboard. That is not a failed write; it is the wrong effect to see it with.

light.unread: Not read from the board yet. Until it is, there is nothing to say which colours are stored.
light.clearHint: Puts the three bytes back to zero — which to the board means no custom colour, not black. Nothing in this app can tell those two apart.
light.applied: Wrote {count} keys and read the bytes back to check
light.noChange: The board already holds these colours, so nothing was sent.
light.mismatch: {count} slots did not read back as written: {detail}
light.unmapped: {count} keys have no slot, so they could be neither read nor written: {keys}
light.hoverNone: Point at a cap to read its colour
light.pickNone: Drag across the caps to pick keys, then choose a colour

live.title: The frame the board is displaying
live.body: 0xde does not read the stored layer in flash — it reads the RAM buffer the firmware has just filled, so it carries whatever effect is running plus the firmware's calibration overlay (an under-calibrated key painted red or amber, spec §3.3). Disagreeing with the stored colours is therefore normal, and this is also the only way to check whether a stored colour is actually reaching the LEDs.
live.poll: With Live on, the frame is re-read every {ms} ms — the stock driver reads the same command every time its job queue empties (spec §3.0). It has no interval of its own, only idle time, so this one is this app's ceiling rather than something copied. Turn it off to hold a single frame still.

effect.body: The effect settings live in <c>payload[17..24]</c> of the global block and in the two 256-byte blocks behind <c>0xa4</c> / <c>0xa6</c>. Which byte is which has not been recovered from the stock driver or from the firmware (spec §9). Filling them in from guesses corrupts the lighting blocks — this project has done exactly that once (findings.md #4) — so this panel stays empty.

debug.hint: Shift {presses} times to change it back

storage.title: What gets stored
storage.hint: The language picked in the top bar, whether debug mode is on, and the sensor addresses you bind on the Events tab live in this browser's localStorage only — they survive closing the browser, and none of them reaches the board. Board settings above are the other way round: they live on the keyboard, so they are the same whichever PC you open this on.

debug.gestureOff: Tap Shift {presses} times quickly to make this tab go away again. These are tools for decoding the protocol, so you do not normally need them.

keyId.title: Key identification
keyId.label: Ignore the built-in table — use my own bindings only
keyId.hint: All 61 keys now name themselves in the event stream (modifiers through the HID modifier bitmask in payload[2]), so this table is only a fallback. It guesses a key from its sensor value and baseline ADC, both of which calibration changes — and a stale table guesses wrong rather than not at all. Turn it off when that happens.

explorer.title: HID explorer
explorer.hint: The report descriptor as the browser parsed it. Check the report ids you can send, and their exact lengths, here.
explorer.chromeNote: Chrome deliberately does not expose the keyboard top-level collections (0x01/0x06) to WebHID. Their absence here is not a fault — configuration goes through the vendor-defined collection.

console.title: Report console
console.payloadPlaceholder: e.g. 55 a9 00 00   (you supply the checksum yourself)
console.badCommand: The command must be in the range 00–ff

reply.ack: ACK — command {command} was received, no data

console.constant: Every byte was identical across {count} repeats — these are constants, not live values.
console.moving: Bytes that moved: {offsets} — those are the live ones.

prober.title: Command prober

warning.title: Careful — this sends commands nobody has identified yet.
warning.body: 0x01 (begin) and 0x02 (end/commit) appear to open and close a settings transaction. What the commands in between write is still unknown, so a settings reset or a flash write is possible. The stock driver warns that this board needs key calibration after a firmware upgrade — meaning a command that touches calibration exists too. Back your settings up with the stock driver first.

prober.knownOnly: Only try the {count} commands the stock driver actually sends (recommended)
prober.safeOnly: Send only the commands confirmed safe ({commands}). The rest are block writes, and sending one with an empty payload can zero the start of a firmware blob.
prober.wrap: Wrap each command in a 0x01 … 0x02 transaction (the stock driver's own order)
prober.acknowledge: I understand the risk and have backed my settings up
prober.noAnswer: Nothing answered. If the stock driver is running it may hold the device exclusively — close it and try again. If that changes nothing, try a different report id or mode.
prober.legend: ★ = a command the stock driver actually sends (0x01 begin, 0x02 end/commit, {globalSettings} global settings) · ⚠ = a command observed to change board state when sent with an empty payload
prober.badRange: That sweep range is not valid (00–ff).

events.title: Event listener
events.intro: Listens to the reports the board sends without being asked. The stock driver polls these in a loop of its own and treats every report starting with 0xa0 as an event. Listening alone sends nothing. The board only streams once it has been armed though (spec §3.2), so if nothing arrives, turn on arm stream below as well. Reporting is enabled and the test mode exited right after, so typing keeps working and nothing is recalibrated.
events.armStream: Arm stream ({arm} → {disarm}) — typing is disabled while arming
events.silent: Nothing has arrived yet. Try pressing a key, and if that changes nothing turn on arm stream — the board sends nothing at all until it is armed.
events.pressHint: Press the keys one at a time. Any key left grey has no sensor address bound to it yet.
events.bindHint: Pick the key to bind from the grid ({fingerprint}).
events.unbound_one: {count} key does not name itself. Modifiers and Fn are reported as a HID bitmask and so carry no usage (0x00, or 0x01 for Fn). Pick one below, then click the matching key in the grid above to bind it. The identity is the sensor value plus the baseline ADC — the sensor value alone collides for some keys.
events.unbound_other: {count} keys do not name themselves. Modifiers and Fn are reported as a HID bitmask and so carry no usage (0x00, or 0x01 for Fn). Pick one below, then click the matching key in the grid above to bind it. The identity is the sensor value plus the baseline ADC — the sensor value alone collides for some keys.
events.notAnalog: Not in the analog key event format
events.noMoving: All {count} were identical — no byte moved.

log.title: Traffic log
log.hint_one: Click a line to mark it A/B and see the byte differences between the two reports. {count} entry.
log.hint_other: Click a line to mark it A/B and see the byte differences between the two reports. {count} entries.

sensors.title: Live key travel · ADC
sensors.intro: Shows exactly what the board sends — live key travel and every raw sensor number behind it (current ADC, the resting baseline ADC, sensor delta, sensor value). The board does not report a key it is not being pressed, so the grid only fills in as you press each key once.
sensors.focus: Focus #{index} {key} — click a key to change it
sensors.uncalibrated: Some keys are not calibrated. They report a total stroke of 0, so the travel shown is an estimate scaled against the nominal {nominal} mm. One calibration pass replaces it with the measured value.
sensors.staleTable: The built-in table does not describe this board. A key that needs fingerprint identification reported a sensor value the table has never heard of, or one sensor value showed more baselines than it has keys. A modifier can resolve to the wrong key in this state — the Sensor values panel in debug mode shows which value is at fault. Turn on Ignore the built-in table in Settings and bind the keys by hand in the Events tab.
sensors.armFailedHint: Check that the interface marked recommended on the Device tab is the one that is open.
sensors.armed: Analog reporting is on (<c>{arm}</c> → <c>{disarm}</c>). Reporting stays enabled while the test mode has been exited, so typing keeps working and nothing is recalibrated.
sensors.gridLegend: The fill is the current travel; the number below it is travel mm / current ADC.
sensors.drifted: The baseline ADC has drifted. A baseline is a stored calibration constant, so a value changing within one session — or more values under one sensor value than it has keys — means a recalibration happened in between. The drift panel below shows how far it is from the built-in table.
sensors.unresolvedHint_one: {count} unresolved identity can be bound to a key on the Events tab.
sensors.unresolvedHint_other: {count} unresolved identities can be bound to keys on the Events tab.
sensors.notAKeyHint: {count} not-a-key reports — no usage, no modifier bits and no baseline ADC ({ids}). A healthy board keeps sending these, so they are left out of key identification.

address.title: Key address candidates — finding a byte that does not drift
address.intro: Taking the {groups} keys that name themselves through a usage as ground truth, every byte is checked two ways: is it always the same value within one key, and does it differ between keys? A byte that does both is a key address that calibration cannot shake.
address.found: An undecoded byte meets the address criteria. If it also differs across the modifiers, keys can be identified by this byte instead of by their fingerprint — regardless of calibration.
address.none: No undecoded byte meets the address criteria. That may just be too few samples, so press each key several times at different depths. If none turns up, this event carries no calibration-safe identifier and modifiers have to rely on your own bindings.
address.unnamedCheck: Whether the candidate bytes really do differ across the unnamed keys (modifiers · Fn):

drift.title: Baseline ADC drift — against the built-in table
drift.intro: For each entry in <c>fingerprints.ts</c>, the closest baseline ADC observed under the same sensor value. The tolerance is ±{tolerance}; beyond that the key either fails to resolve or resolves to a different key.

note.ambiguous: indistinguishable from another key on the same sensor value
note.outOfRange: outside tolerance — this key will not resolve

drift.copySource: Copy the updated table as source
drift.copyHint: Rewrites <c>KEY_FINGERPRINTS</c> with the observed baseline ADCs — key assignments stay as they are, only the numbers change.
drift.ambiguous: Some pairs are ambiguous. Two keys under the same sensor value have observations close enough that this table alone cannot say which observation belongs to which key. Bind those keys yourself on the Events tab by pressing them one at a time — your own bindings win over the built-in table.

trace.title: Trace — #{index} {key}
trace.noise: resting jitter {mm} mm — rapid trigger sensitivity must be larger than this

sensorTable.title: Sensor values vs the built-in table
sensorTable.intro: Every sensor value observed (payload[12..13]), with whether the built-in table knows it. A value missing from the table is not a problem for a key identified by its usage or modifier bit — the table is only the fallback for when both of those fail.

bottomOut.title: Always trigger on bottom-out (global)
bottomOut.enable: Always trigger when the key bottoms out
bottomOut.hint: The only rapid-trigger setting that is not per key. It sits in the 32-byte global block at payload[15] bit 1, so it has its own read and write (0x05 / 0x06). That block also holds settings belonging to other screens — polling rate, dead zone, game lock, the lighting effect — so the block is read, this one bit is flipped, and it is written back. Same as the stock driver does.
bottomOut.applied: Applied, and the global block was read back to confirm.
bottomOut.noChange: The board already held this value, so nothing was sent.
bottomOut.mismatch: The byte read back differently from what was written: {detail}
bottomOut.raw: payload[15] = {byte} · Tachyon {tachyon} · actuation_check {actuationCheck} · magnet test {magnetTest} · debounce {debounce}
